transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-26
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Tom Nguyen (Redwood AE), Sofia Ramirez (Redwood SE), Marcus Li (Redwood SRE), Aisha Park (Redwood CSM), Rachel Summers (CobaltPay CTO), Jamal Ortiz (Eng Mgr), Priya Shah (Platform Lead), Ethan Cole (SRE)

Summary:
Quick checkpoint in week 3 of the pilot. Reviewed yesterday's throughput run which showed steady-state improvements when continuous batching was enabled but a tail latency regression during bursts. Agreed action items: customer to provide production traffic histogram; Redwood SE to push an updated batching profile and tracing; Redwood AE to share capacity/price sketch for potential dedicated reservation. Discussed concurrency targets, queue governor (backpressure) settings, and fallback to smaller quantized variant for cost vs latency tradeoff.

Topics:
- Continuous batching tuning and sample configs
- Concurrency targets and request queueing/backpressure
- Burst behavior and fallbacks (model variants)
- Observability: traces, token-level latency buckets, cost breakdown
- Next steps and owners

Transcript body:
[00:00] Tom Nguyen: okay everybody thanks for joining i think we have a pretty full agenda, i'll kick off and then hand to sofia for the perf bits.
[00:18] Rachel Summers: thanks tom, quick note — we only have the SREs on until 11:15 so if we need deep tracing data we might have to timebox that.
[00:26] Tom Nguyen: good call, we'll prioritize the throughput run findings first. sofia over to you.
[00:32] Sofia Ramirez: yeah thanks, so last 24-hour run — we toggled continuous batching on with a conservative batch timeout (10ms) and raised the local concurrency target from 8 to 12 per worker. baseline was our week-1 run. what we saw: token/sec improved ~18% steady-state, average cost per 1k tokens down, but p99 tail latency moved from 420ms to 720ms during burst windows.
[01:05] Jamal Ortiz: when you say burst windows is that related to queue depth? like do requests pile up and then flush?
[01:12] Sofia Ramirez: yeah exactly, we saw queue depth spikes — the runtime batches more aggressively which amortizes work but if there's an immediate spike the queueing delay added plus longer KV cache warmups caused the tail. some of the p99s are actually KV warmup not attention compute.
[01:32] Priya Shah: K-V cash? you mean the kv cache for the transformer keys? sometimes our logs call it the key cache.
[01:38] Sofia Ramirez: yes kv cache (sorry i said "K-V cash"). good point — warmups matter. we instrumented token-level traces and you can see misses at the start of a burst.
[01:48] Marcus Li: we also had an experiment where enabling backpressure/queue governor at the front end limited inflight requests to 16 per node and that bounded the p99 back to ~480ms but reduced observed throughput by ~6% during sustained high load.
[02:10] Rachel Summers: so that suggests a tradeoff — we can keep higher throughput but accept higher tail latencies, or throttle slightly to get stable latency. our product SLAs want p99 under 600ms for the payments flow.
[02:24] Tom Nguyen: exactly — that's the governance decision. for pilot we need to aim for two operating points: a throughput-first mode for batch processing and a latency-first mode for real-time payments. we can implement automatic routing by route or by header to choose the target.
[02:41] Ethan Cole: technically how heavy is switching? can we change concurrency targets on the fly without restarting pods?
[02:48] Sofia Ramirez: yes you can adjust concurrency targets in the agent control plane; it's a soft limit so it applies on next allocation slice, no pod restart. latency to effect is seconds.
[02:56] Jamal Ortiz: nice. what about continuous batching config — we used 10ms earlier, could we try 6ms or adaptive timeouts?
[03:03] Sofia Ramirez: adaptive is what we recommend — increase the timeout when queue is empty, shrink when queue backlog grows. we can push a tuned profile that adjusts batch windows based on percentiles of inter-arrival times.
[03:17] Priya Shah: would that be safe for our tail? i'm worried adaptive could increase variance.
[03:22] Sofia Ramirez: fair. the profile has hysteresis and max batch cap to avoid runaway. also pairing it with a small request-level timeout for latency-sensitive routes helps.
[03:32] Rachel Summers: can you remind us where fallback model variants come in? sometimes we degrade to a smaller quantized model to save latency and cost, right?
[03:40] Sofia Ramirez: yep — fallback chain is a configured policy. e.g., if p99 latency exceeds 800ms or queue depth > 40 for >30s we can route to a quantized 4-bit variant that has lower per-token latency but slightly lower quality.
[03:55] Jamal Ortiz: what's the quality hit, any eval numbers?
[03:58] Sofia Ramirez: in our internal eval for this workload we saw negligible regression on extraction tasks, for generative completions it was noticeable in long-coherent threads. we can share the eval deck.
[04:12] Marcus Li: on observability — to make decisions we need token-level latency buckets, not just request-level. that helps us diagnose kv miss vs compute. can you instrument that?
[04:21] Sofia Ramirez: yes we've already added token-bucket traces in the last run, i'll attach sample traces. they show start-of-request kv miss spikes for about the first 8 tokens in large bursts.
[04:33] Priya Shah: we'll export our production traffic histogram today — timestamps+interarrival times, should be helpful. will post by EOD.
[04:41] Tom Nguyen: great. two experiments we agreed on: 1) adaptive batch window + max batch cap; 2) front-end queue governor limiting inflight per node and a canary of fallback to quantized variant at 1% traffic to measure quality impact.
[04:58] Rachel Summers: for the canary, is it easy to route 1%? we use our own load balancer.
[05:03] Marcus Li: yes we can do it at the request router via header or path prefix, or Redwood can accept a routing header. elasticity is straightforward.
[05:10] Jamal Ortiz: about cost — if we increase concurrency targets, do we need more GPU footprint and hence cost?
[05:16] Sofia Ramirez: concurrency increases throughput per node up to a point. you can usually get better GPU utilization which lowers cost per token. but if you pick too high concurrency you might hit memory or kernel saturation and see worse p99. it's workload dependent.
[05:31] Tom Nguyen: i'll send a sketch of what dedicated commitment looks like and a ballpark pricing range assuming your current qps and the two operating points.
[05:39] Rachel Summers: thanks. also we briefly considered competitor setups — our infra team was looking at Anthropic and an in-house model host; main concern was private network/EKS integration and audit logs. Redwood's private/vpc offering was a plus.
[05:56] Tom Nguyen: good to know. on audit logs we can show sample schema — SSO and KMS integration are supported.
[06:03] Priya Shah: small thing — SAML is mandatory for us, any blockers there?
[06:07] Aisha Park: we support SAML/SSO, we've integrated with Okta for other customers, we can share setup docs.
[06:12] Priya Shah: perfect.
[06:13] Sofia Ramirez: back to experiments — i propose we push the adaptive batching profile to canary nodes (20%) and run a 6-hour ramp to observe p50/p95/p99 and token throughput. then flip queue governor on in the second half.
[06:27] Jamal Ortiz: agreed. what metrics do we need in the dashboard to decide success?
[06:31] Sofia Ramirez: p50/p95/p99 token latency, throughput tokens/sec, average batch size, kv cache hit ratio, queue depth, and cost per 1k tokens. also the quality regression metric for the 1% fallback — we'll collect a small eval set.
[06:46] Rachel Summers: timeline?
[06:49] Tom Nguyen: can we commit to running the 6-hour canary tomorrow and post results by end of day?
[06:54] Priya Shah: yes we can run tomorrow AM and post results by EOD.
[06:58] Sofia Ramirez: i'll prepare the profile and tracing instrumentation tonight, share it by tomorrow 09:00.
[07:04] Marcus Li: i'll kick off the stress test with backpressure enabled and post logs — tentative run Monday if that works.
[07:12] Jamal Ortiz: one more question — how do we tune autoscaling so we don't overprovision when bursts subside?
[07:18] Sofia Ramirez: autoscaler should use request-based signals (tokens/sec) and a cooldown window; also combine with queue-depth-based scale-in suppression to avoid flapping. we recommend a 3-minute cooldown for scale-in.
[07:32] Priya Shah: ok we'll try that in the config.
[07:35] Rachel Summers: any gotchas with ephemeral KV cache in the private deployment? we sometimes see cold-starts after rolling updates.
[07:43] Marcus Li: yes rolling updates can flush local KV; you can use sticky routing or warmup probes to rebuild cache proactively.
[07:52] Sofia Ramirez: or use a shared warmup job that replays representative requests after deploy. we've had success with that.
[08:00] Tom Nguyen: great discussion. let's do the recap.
[08:03] Recap (Tom Nguyen): 1) Customer will run 24h histogram export + 6-hour canary tomorrow (Priya to post by EOD). 2) Redwood SE (Sofia) will push adaptive batching profile and tracing by 09:00 tomorrow. 3) Marcus to run stress/backpressure test and post logs early next week. 4) Tom to send dedicated capacity/pricing sketch by 2026-03-31. 5) All to reconvene next Wednesday for post-canary review.
[08:33] Priya Shah: confirmed. we'll also include example interarrival times and any production routing headers.
[08:40] Tom Nguyen: perfect. thanks everyone, i'll follow up with calendar invite for Weds.
[08:44] Rachel Summers: thank you.
[08:46] Meeting ends
